sectionTitle: Energy changes in a system, and the ways energy is stored before and after such changes — part 4.1.1.1

specStatements.text: A system is an object or group of objects.
There are changes in the way energy is stored when a system changes.
Students should be able to describe all the changes involved in the way energy is stored when a system changes, for common situations. For example:
• a moving object hitting an obstacle
• an object accelerated by a constant force
• bringing water to a boil in an electric kettle.
Throughout this section on Energy students should be able to calculate the changes in energy involved when a system is changed by:
• work done when a current flows
• use calculations to show on a common scale how the overall energy in a system is redistributed when the system is changed.

scopeNotes.statement: Throughout this section on Energy students should be able to calculate the changes in energy involved when a system is changed by:
scopeNotes.howHonoured: This is a signposting statement: the three routes are named here, but the equations themselves are set out in later parts of the Energy section and in 4.5.2. Only those equations are used — ΔE = m c Δθ, W = F s and P = E/t — and their status is respected. W = F s and P = E/t must be recalled; ΔE = m c Δθ is supplied on the Physics equation sheet and the stem says so whenever it is needed. No equation from outside the Energy section (other than the work done equation the specification itself names) is introduced, and no numerical value of specific heat capacity is expected from memory — every question supplies it.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to describe all the changes involved in the way energy is stored when a system changes, for common situations. For example:
scopeNotes.howHonoured: 'For example' marks the five bullets as exemplars of common situations, not a closed list. Every question here is set in one of the five named situations or in a directly equivalent everyday one, and the demand is always to describe the changes in the way energy is stored. Nothing is asked that belongs to later sub-sections: efficiency, the formal statement of conservation and dissipation of energy (4.1.2), power (4.1.1.5) and the national grid are not tested, even where the context could invite them.

concepts.definition: A system is an object or group of objects. It is whatever you decide to treat as the thing you are studying — a single ball, or a ball and the Earth, or a kettle together with the water in it. Choosing the system first is what makes it possible to say clearly which stores are emptying and which are filling.

Energy in a system is described as being held in stores. When a system changes, there are changes in the way energy is stored: the amount of energy in some stores goes down and the amount in others goes up.

concepts.term: The energy stores used in this specification
concepts.definition: The stores named across the AQA specification are: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, magnetic, electrostatic and nuclear. Heating, work done by forces, work done when a current flows and radiation are not stores — they are the ways energy gets from one store to another.

concepts.term: Describing all the changes in a system
concepts.definition: A full description names the store or stores that empty, the store or stores that fill, and the way the energy was transferred between them. 'All the changes' includes the small ones — the thermal stores of the surroundings that fill because of friction or air resistance are part of the answer, not an optional extra.

As the object rises, its kinetic store empties and its gravitational potential store fills; air resistance also fills the thermal store of the object and the surroundings. At the highest point the object is momentarily at rest, so its kinetic store is empty and its gravitational potential store is at its largest. On the way down the changes run the other way.

concepts.term: A moving object hitting an obstacle
concepts.definition: The kinetic store of the moving object empties. Energy fills the thermal stores of the object, of the obstacle and of the surroundings, and some is carried away by sound waves. If either object is squashed and springs back, an elastic potential store fills and then empties again.

concepts.term: An object accelerated by a constant force
concepts.definition: The force does work on the object as the object moves. Work done by the force fills the kinetic store of the object, so the object speeds up. Because work done = force × distance, acting over a longer distance transfers more energy to the kinetic store, even though the force is unchanged.

The kinetic store of the vehicle empties. Friction forces in the brakes do work, filling the thermal store of the brakes; friction at the tyres and air resistance fill thermal stores too. The hot brakes then transfer energy to the thermal store of the surroundings as they cool.

concepts.term: Bringing water to a boil in an electric kettle
concepts.definition: A current flows in the heating element, so work is done and the thermal store of the element fills. The element heats the water, filling the thermal store of the water. The thermal stores of the kettle body and of the surrounding room also fill, and once the water boils, energy is carried away by the escaping steam.

concepts.term: The three ways a system is changed
concepts.definition: Throughout the Energy section, the energy change when a system is changed is calculated for three routes: heating, work done by forces, and work done when a current flows. Each is a way of transferring energy into or out of stores, and each is measured in joules.

concepts.term: Calculating an energy change by heating
concepts.definition: ΔE = m c Δθ, that is change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change, with ΔE in joules (J), m in kilograms (kg), c in J/kg °C and Δθ in °C. This equation is supplied on the Physics equation sheet, so it does not have to be recalled — but Δθ is the change in temperature, not the final temperature.

concepts.term: Calculating work done by a force
concepts.definition: W = F s, that is work done = force × distance (along the line of action of the force), with W in joules (J), F in newtons (N) and s in metres (m). This equation must be recalled. If the object does not move along the line of action of the force, no work is done by that force, however large the force is.

concepts.term: Calculating work done when a current flows
concepts.definition: P = E/t, that is power = energy transferred / time, with P in watts (W), E in joules (J) and t in seconds (s). This equation must be recalled, and it rearranges to E = P t. Time must be in seconds: a three-minute boil is 180 s, not 3.

Every energy change — by heating, by work done by forces, or by work done when a current flows — is measured in the same unit, the joule (J). That shared unit is what makes it possible to put all the changes in one system side by side and compare them directly.

concepts.term: Showing redistribution on a common scale
concepts.definition: Once each change has been calculated in joules, the amounts can be drawn as bars on one shared scale, showing how the energy in the system was redistributed. The energy is not lost or created: the amounts shown after the change add up to the amount shown before it, spread differently among the stores.

misconceptions.question: Does a system have to be a machine or a device?
misconceptions.correct: No. A system is simply an object or group of objects — a stone, a beaker of water, or a car and the road it drives on.
misconceptions.misconception: A system is a machine or a piece of equipment, like an engine or a circuit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'system' is used in everyday life for heating systems, sound systems and computer systems, all of which are built devices.
misconceptions.correction: In physics the word is deliberately much wider. The specification defines it in one line: a system is an object or group of objects. You choose the system; nothing has to be manufactured for it to count.

misconceptions.question: Can a single object on its own be a system?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The definition allows an object or a group of objects, so one ball on its own is a perfectly good system.
misconceptions.misconception: A system has to be more than one thing, because things have to interact for anything to happen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most worked examples involve two or more objects, and the word 'group' in the definition is the part students remember.
misconceptions.correction: Read the definition carefully: 'an object or group of objects'. Both are allowed. Choosing a single object as the system is often the simplest way to describe a change.

misconceptions.question: When a car brakes to a stop, is its energy used up?
misconceptions.correct: No. The energy is transferred to other stores — mainly the thermal stores of the brakes and the surroundings.
misconceptions.misconception: Energy gets used up when a system changes, so there is less of it afterwards.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language talks about 'using energy' and 'running out of energy', and the useful effect really does disappear.
misconceptions.correction: What runs out is the energy in one particular store, not the energy itself. When a system changes, some stores empty and others fill. The specification's phrase is 'changes in the way energy is stored'.

misconceptions.question: Is 'heat energy' or 'sound energy' an energy store?
misconceptions.correct: No. Heating and sound waves are ways energy is transferred. The stores include thermal, kinetic, chemical, gravitational potential and elastic potential.
misconceptions.misconception: There are different types of energy — heat energy, light energy, sound energy, electrical energy — and they change into each other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Primary and lower-secondary teaching often uses a list of 'types of energy', and the phrase 'changes into' is hard to unlearn.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the two ideas. Stores hold energy; transfers move it. Sound, light, heating and a current flowing are transfers, not stores. A description should say which store emptied, which store filled, and by which route.

misconceptions.question: A ball is thrown straight up. Does its kinetic store still hold energy at the very top?
misconceptions.correct: No. At the highest point the ball is momentarily at rest, so its kinetic store is empty and its gravitational potential store is at its largest.
misconceptions.misconception: The ball must still have kinetic energy at the top, otherwise there would be nothing to bring it back down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students link 'having energy' with 'being able to move next', and it feels as though the throw must still be pushing the ball.
misconceptions.correction: What brings the ball back down is the weight acting on it, not a leftover kinetic store. At the top the gravitational potential store is full; on the way down that store empties and the kinetic store fills again.

misconceptions.question: When is the gravitational potential store of a ball thrown upwards at its largest?
misconceptions.correct: At the top of its flight, where it is highest above the ground.
misconceptions.misconception: It is largest the moment the ball leaves the hand, because that is when the ball is moving fastest.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'most energy' with 'fastest', and do not separate the two stores; leaving the hand feels like the moment of greatest effort.
misconceptions.correction: The gravitational potential store depends on height, not speed. At launch the ball is low and fast, so its kinetic store is at its largest; at the top it is high and stationary, so its gravitational potential store is at its largest.

misconceptions.question: A trolley crashes into a wall and stops. What happens to the energy in its kinetic store?
misconceptions.correct: It is transferred, mainly filling the thermal stores of the trolley, the wall and the surroundings, with some carried away by sound waves.
misconceptions.misconception: The kinetic energy is destroyed by the impact — that is what stopping means.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The motion visibly ends, and nothing obvious appears in its place, so 'destroyed' seems to describe what happened.
misconceptions.correction: The motion ends, but the energy does not. Crumpled metal, warm brakes, a warm wall and a bang are all evidence of stores that filled. Describing the change means naming those stores.

misconceptions.question: When a moving object hits an obstacle, does all the energy go into the obstacle?
misconceptions.correct: No. Thermal stores of the moving object, of the obstacle and of the surroundings all fill, and sound waves carry some energy away.
misconceptions.misconception: The energy is passed on to the thing that was hit, in the same way a ball passes motion to another ball.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Collisions between snooker balls, where motion really is passed on, are the model students carry into every collision.
misconceptions.correction: Only when the obstacle moves off does its kinetic store fill. When an object hits a wall or a hedge and stops, the change is mostly into thermal stores on both sides of the collision plus sound.

misconceptions.question: A constant force pushes a trolley along a smooth bench. Does the kinetic store stay the same?
misconceptions.correct: No. A constant force does work as the trolley moves, so the trolley accelerates and its kinetic store keeps filling.
misconceptions.misconception: A constant force gives a constant amount of energy, so the trolley moves at a steady speed and its kinetic store does not change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Constant' is read as 'steady', and everyday pushing of heavy objects at walking pace really does give constant speed, because friction balances the push.
misconceptions.correction: Constant force means unchanging force, not unchanging speed. With no opposing force the trolley accelerates, and the work done by the force — force × distance — keeps filling the kinetic store.

misconceptions.question: Is work done whenever a force is applied?
misconceptions.correct: No. Work is done only when the object moves along the line of action of the force. No movement means no work done by that force.
misconceptions.misconception: If I push hard on something, I am doing work on it, whether or not it moves.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday meaning of 'work' is effort, and applying a force certainly takes effort.
misconceptions.correction: The specification defines work done = force × distance (along the line of action of the force). If the distance is zero, the work done on the object is zero, no matter how big the force.

misconceptions.question: Do the brakes destroy the kinetic energy of a car?
misconceptions.correct: No. Friction forces in the brakes do work, transferring energy from the kinetic store of the car into the thermal store of the brakes.
misconceptions.misconception: Braking gets rid of the energy — the friction cancels it out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'friction' is taught as something that opposes and reduces motion, so it is easy to treat it as removing energy from existence.
misconceptions.correction: Friction is a force, and forces do work: they move energy between stores. Racing car brakes glow red hot, which is direct evidence of the thermal store filling.

misconceptions.question: After a car has stopped, where does the energy in the hot brakes go?
misconceptions.correct: The brakes cool down, transferring energy to the thermal store of the surroundings.
misconceptions.misconception: The energy stays in the brakes, because that is where it went when the car stopped.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students stop the description at the moment the car stops, and the later cooling is slow and invisible.
misconceptions.correction: 'All the changes' includes what happens afterwards. Anything hotter than its surroundings transfers energy to them until the temperatures match, so the thermal store of the surroundings finishes larger.

misconceptions.question: Does a kettle contain a store of electrical energy?
misconceptions.correct: No. There is no electrical store. A current flowing does work, and that fills the thermal stores of the element and then the water.
misconceptions.misconception: Electricity is a kind of energy that is stored in the mains, the wires or the appliance until it is used.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Phrases such as 'electrical energy' and 'using electricity' are everywhere, and a charged battery does behave like a store — but it is a chemical store.
misconceptions.correction: The current is the route, not the store. Work is done when a current flows, and that fills a store somewhere else — usually a thermal store or a kinetic store in a motor.

misconceptions.question: Does all the energy transferred by a kettle end up in the water?
misconceptions.correct: No. Most of it fills the thermal store of the water, but the thermal stores of the kettle body and of the room also fill, and steam carries some away.
misconceptions.misconception: The kettle is designed to heat the water, so all the energy goes into the water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The intended effect is the only one that gets mentioned, and the other transfers are small and hard to see.
misconceptions.correction: A kettle body is warm after boiling, and steam leaves the spout — both are stores that filled. Describing all the changes means listing these as well as the water.

misconceptions.question: Water is heated from 20 °C to 100 °C. What value of Δθ goes into ΔE = m c Δθ?
misconceptions.correct: Δθ = 80 °C, the change in temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: Δθ is the temperature the water reaches, so you use 100 °C.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The final temperature is the number the question is 'about', and the Greek letter delta is unfamiliar, so it gets ignored.
misconceptions.correction: The Δ symbol means 'change in'. Subtract the starting temperature from the final one: 100 − 20 = 80 °C. Using 100 would give an answer far too large.

misconceptions.question: Can the mass be left out of ΔE = m c Δθ if you know the substance?
misconceptions.correct: No. Specific heat capacity is the energy needed per kilogram, so the mass must be multiplied in.
misconceptions.misconception: The specific heat capacity already tells you about the water, so multiplying by 4200 and the temperature change is enough.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'specific' is not read as 'per kilogram', so c looks like a property that covers the whole sample.
misconceptions.correction: c = 4200 J/kg °C means 4200 joules for each kilogram for each degree. Heating 0.5 kg needs half as much as heating 1 kg, so the mass has to appear in the calculation.

misconceptions.question: On a common-scale diagram, do the amounts after the change have to add up to the amount before?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The energy is redistributed among the stores, so the totals before and after match.
misconceptions.misconception: The bars after the change do not have to add up to the bar before, because energy is used up or shared out unevenly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The diagram is treated as a picture of what happened rather than as a set of calculated numbers that must balance.
misconceptions.correction: The point of the common scale is that the joules can be added. Work out each change in joules, and check that the amounts afterwards total the amount you started with — that is what 'redistributed' means.

misconceptions.question: Can an energy change caused by heating be compared with one caused by work done by a force?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Both are energy changes measured in joules, so they can be drawn on the same scale and added.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating and work done by forces are different kinds of thing, so their values cannot be put on one scale.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two are calculated with different equations and taught in different lessons, so they feel like different quantities.
misconceptions.correction: Different routes, same quantity. ΔE = m c Δθ, W = F s and E = P t all give an answer in joules, which is exactly why a single common scale works.

misconceptions.question: Does the mass of an object appear in the equation for work done by a force?
misconceptions.correct: No. Work done = force × distance. The mass is not part of it.
misconceptions.misconception: You multiply force by mass by distance, because a heavier object takes more energy to move.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mass appears in most other energy equations the students have met, and questions often supply a mass, which looks like an instruction to use it.
misconceptions.correction: W = F s uses only the force and the distance moved along its line of action. A mass given in a work-done question is often there for a different part of the question, or as a check that you know what to ignore.

misconceptions.question: A 2000 W heater runs for 3.0 minutes. What time goes into E = P t?
misconceptions.correct: 180 s. Time must be converted to seconds.
misconceptions.misconception: You put 3 into the equation, because the heater was on for 3 minutes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number in the question is 3, and the unit is not treated as part of the quantity.
misconceptions.correction: A watt is a joule per second, so t must be in seconds for the answer to be in joules. 3.0 minutes × 60 = 180 s, giving 360 000 J rather than 6000 J.

misconceptions.question: Is 'energy is transferred' a full description of a change in a system?
misconceptions.correct: No. You must say which store empties, which store or stores fill, and how the energy was transferred.
misconceptions.misconception: Saying that energy is transferred, or that it moves from one place to another, answers the question.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase sounds like correct physics vocabulary, and it is often accepted in class discussion.
misconceptions.correction: The specification asks for all the changes in the way energy is stored. Name the stores: for a ball rolling down a slope, the gravitational potential store empties while the kinetic store and thermal stores fill.

misconceptions.question: Can a stationary object have energy in its stores?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A stationary object can have full chemical, thermal, elastic potential or gravitational potential stores.
misconceptions.misconception: Only moving things have energy, so a hedge, a wall or a book on a shelf has none.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Kinetic energy is usually met first, and 'energy' is popularly associated with activity and movement.
misconceptions.correction: Motion fills only one store. A hot wall, a stretched spring, a lump of coal and a book on a high shelf all hold energy while completely still, and their stores can gain energy in a collision.

misconceptions.question: You hold a heavy box still at arm's length for 30 s. How much work do you do on the box?
misconceptions.correct: None. The box does not move along the line of action of the force, so no work is done on it.
misconceptions.misconception: Holding it is exhausting and gets harder the longer you hold it, so a lot of work must be being done on the box.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Muscles really do empty a chemical store while holding a load, so the effort is genuine — it just is not work done on the box.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish the two systems. Inside your arm, energy is transferred as muscle fibres repeatedly contract. On the box, force × distance = force × 0 = 0 J. Time does not appear in W = F s at all.

misconceptions.question: Is the current used up as it flows through a heating element?
misconceptions.correct: No. The current is the same all the way round a series circuit; it is energy that is transferred, not current.
misconceptions.misconception: The current is used up by the element, which is why the element gets hot and the wire beyond it is cool.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Something clearly gets 'used' at the element, and current and energy are both invisible, so the two ideas merge.
misconceptions.correction: Charge is not consumed. What happens is work done when a current flows, filling the thermal store of the element. Say 'energy is transferred', never 'current is used up'.

misconceptions.question: Why must the bars on an energy diagram share one scale?
misconceptions.correct: So that the sizes can be compared and added directly, showing how the total has been redistributed.
misconceptions.misconception: Each store can be drawn on its own scale, as long as every bar is labelled with its value.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In other subjects, charts are drawn to fill the space, and small quantities are often shown on a stretched axis so they can be seen.
misconceptions.correction: The specification asks for a common scale precisely so that a small change looks small. Separate scales hide the fact that the amounts before and after must add up to the same total.

misconceptions.question: P = E/t. How do you rearrange it to find the energy transferred?
misconceptions.correct: E = P t — multiply the power by the time.
misconceptions.misconception: You keep the division and write E = P/t, because the equation has a divide in it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rearranging is done by pattern-matching the symbols rather than by doing the same operation to both sides.
misconceptions.correction: Multiply both sides by t: P × t = E. Check with units — watts × seconds = joules, whereas watts ÷ seconds is not an energy at all.

mcqs.stem: In physics, what is meant by a system?

options.text: An object or a group of objects.
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition, word for word.

options.text: A machine that transfers energy.
options.rationale: The everyday meaning of 'system' as a built device is carried into physics.

options.text: A group of objects, never just one.
options.rationale: The word 'group' is remembered but the alternative 'an object' is not.

options.text: A place where energy is kept.
options.rationale: System and store are treated as the same idea; a store is a way energy is held, not the thing being studied.

mcqs.stem: The specification says there are changes in the way energy is stored when a system changes. Which statement describes this correctly?

options.text: Energy is gradually used up as the system changes.
options.rationale: Everyday talk of 'using energy' makes disappearance sound like the natural outcome.

options.text: Some stores empty while other stores fill up.
options.rationale: This is exactly what a change in the way energy is stored means.

options.text: Energy is changed into a different type of energy.
options.rationale: 'Types of energy changing into each other' is the phrasing many students bring from earlier teaching.

options.text: New energy is created somewhere in the system.
options.rationale: Sources such as batteries and fuels look like places where energy is made rather than stored.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is an energy store?

options.text: Heating a beaker of water with a flame.
options.rationale: Heating is often called 'heat energy' and mistaken for a store.

options.text: A current flowing through a heater wire.
options.rationale: 'Electrical energy' is widely spoken of as though it were stored in the current.

options.text: The kinetic store of a moving trolley.
options.rationale: Kinetic is one of the stores named in the specification, and the trolley holds energy in it.

options.text: Sound waves spreading out from a bell.
options.rationale: Sound appears on the old 'types of energy' list, so it is read as a store rather than a transfer.

mcqs.stem: A ball rolls down a slope. Which description best meets the requirement to describe all the changes in the way energy is stored?

options.text: Gravitational potential energy changes into kinetic energy.
options.rationale: The 'changes into' phrasing sounds right and is what many students were taught first.

options.text: Energy is transferred from the top of the slope to the bottom.
options.rationale: It uses correct-sounding vocabulary while naming no store at all.

options.text: The ball uses up its energy as it rolls down to the bottom.
options.rationale: Everyday language about using energy up feels like a description of what happened.

options.text: The gravitational store empties; the kinetic and thermal stores fill.
options.rationale: It names the store that empties, the stores that fill, and includes the thermal store filled by friction.

mcqs.stem: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. Which describes the changes in the way energy is stored as it rises?

options.text: The kinetic store empties and the gravitational potential store fills.
options.rationale: The ball slows as it gains height, so the kinetic store empties as the gravitational potential store fills.

options.text: The gravitational potential store empties and the kinetic store fills up.
options.rationale: Students who link 'most energy' with 'fastest' put the gravitational store at its largest at launch.

options.text: The kinetic store and the gravitational potential store both keep filling.
options.rationale: Students who think the ball keeps its kinetic energy see both stores growing.

options.text: The kinetic store empties and the elastic potential store fills instead.
options.rationale: Elastic potential is confused with gravitational potential because both are called 'potential'.

mcqs.stem: At the highest point of its flight, a ball thrown straight upwards is momentarily at rest. What is true of its energy stores at that moment?

options.text: Its kinetic store still holds energy, or it could not fall back down.
options.rationale: Students think something must be left in the ball to make the next stage of motion happen.

options.text: Its gravitational store is at its largest and its kinetic store is empty.
options.rationale: It is at its greatest height and is not moving, so the gravitational store is full and the kinetic store empty.

options.text: Its gravitational store is empty because it has stopped moving up.
options.rationale: The gravitational store is wrongly tied to motion rather than to height.

options.text: Both its kinetic and gravitational stores are empty at that instant.
options.rationale: 'Momentarily at rest' is read as 'nothing is happening', so both stores are assumed to be zero.

mcqs.stem: A moving trolley crashes into a wall and stops. Which describes the main change in the way energy is stored?

options.text: The kinetic store of the trolley is destroyed by the wall impact.
options.rationale: The motion visibly ends and nothing obvious replaces it, so 'destroyed' feels right.

options.text: The kinetic store passes into the kinetic store of the wall itself.
options.rationale: The snooker-ball model of collisions is applied to a wall that does not move.

options.text: The kinetic store empties into thermal stores of both objects.
options.rationale: The trolley and the wall both warm slightly, and the surroundings do too; this is where the energy goes.

options.text: The kinetic store of the trolley becomes a store of sound waves.
options.rationale: The bang is obvious, and sound is remembered as a 'type of energy' rather than a transfer.

mcqs.stem: A cyclist rides into a hedge and stops. A student says all the energy has gone into the hedge. Why is this description incomplete?

options.text: A hedge cannot store energy because a hedge does not move.
options.rationale: Energy is associated only with motion, so a stationary object is assumed to have no stores.

options.text: The cyclist's kinetic store is used up, not transferred at all.
options.rationale: 'Used up' is the everyday account of what happens when motion stops.

options.text: The kinetic store of the hedge fills as the cyclist stops.
options.rationale: Motion is assumed to be handed on to whatever is hit, even when that object stays still.

options.text: Thermal stores of the cyclist, bike and surroundings also fill.
options.rationale: Energy fills thermal stores on both sides of the collision, plus the surroundings, and sound carries some away.

mcqs.stem: A constant horizontal force pushes a box along a very smooth floor. Which describes the change in the way energy is stored?

options.text: Work done by the force fills the kinetic store of the box.
options.rationale: The force acts along the direction of movement, so it does work and the box accelerates.

options.text: The kinetic store of the box stays the same as it keeps moving.
options.rationale: 'Constant force' is read as 'constant speed', which would mean no change in the kinetic store.

options.text: The gravitational store of the box fills as it is pushed.
options.rationale: Any push is assumed to fill a 'potential' store, even though the box does not rise.

options.text: The energy from the push is used up as the box moves.
options.rationale: Pushing is tiring, so the energy is assumed to be consumed rather than transferred.

mcqs.stem: The same constant force accelerates a trolley over twice the distance. How does this change the energy transferred to the kinetic store?

options.text: It stays the same, because the force has not changed.
options.rationale: Work is thought to depend on the force alone, with distance playing no part.

options.text: It doubles, because work done is force times distance.
options.rationale: W = F s, so doubling s with F unchanged doubles the energy transferred.

options.text: It halves, because the force is spread over more distance.
options.rationale: 'Spread out' is read as 'diluted', as if a fixed amount of energy were being shared over the journey.

options.text: It doubles, but only if the trolley is twice as heavy.
options.rationale: Mass is wrongly believed to belong in the work done equation.

mcqs.stem: A driver brakes and the car slows down. Which describes the changes in the way energy is stored?

options.text: The kinetic store empties and is used up by the brakes.
options.rationale: Braking is described in everyday terms as getting rid of the energy.

options.text: The kinetic store is destroyed by the friction in the brakes.
options.rationale: Friction is taught as something that opposes motion, so it is treated as removing energy.

options.text: The kinetic store empties and thermal stores of the brakes fill.
options.rationale: Friction forces in the brakes do work, filling their thermal store; the tyres and air do so too.

options.text: The kinetic store empties into the gravitational store of the car.
options.rationale: Any 'lost' kinetic energy is assumed to reappear in the other store students know by name.

mcqs.stem: A few minutes after a car has braked and stopped, its brakes have cooled back down. What has happened to the energy?

options.text: It has been destroyed as the brakes cooled down again afterwards.
options.rationale: Cooling looks like the energy simply ceasing to exist.

options.text: It has gone back into the kinetic store of the car that stopped.
options.rationale: Energy is expected to return to where it came from, even though the car is stationary.

options.text: It stays in the thermal store of the brakes for ever afterwards.
options.rationale: The description is stopped at the moment the car stops, ignoring what happens afterwards.

options.text: It has been transferred to thermal stores in the surroundings.
options.rationale: Anything hotter than its surroundings transfers energy to them until the temperatures match.

mcqs.stem: Water is brought to the boil in an electric kettle. Which describes the changes in the way energy is stored?

options.text: Work is done as a current flows; the water's thermal store fills.
options.rationale: A current in the element does work, filling the thermal store of the element and then of the water.

options.text: The electrical store of the kettle empties into the water.
options.rationale: 'Electrical energy' is spoken of as something stored in the appliance or the mains.

options.text: The chemical store of the water fills up as it gets hotter.
options.rationale: Any change in a substance is assumed to be a chemical one, so the wrong store is named.

options.text: Heat energy is made in the element and stored in the water.
options.rationale: 'Heat energy' is treated as a substance that can be manufactured and then held.

mcqs.stem: A kettle boils a full jug of water. Which statement about where the energy ends up is correct?

options.text: All of it goes into the thermal store of the water inside the kettle.
options.rationale: Only the intended effect is considered, so the other transfers are left out.

options.text: Most goes to the water's thermal store, some to the kettle and room.
options.rationale: The kettle body is warm afterwards and steam escapes, so those stores fill as well as the water's.

options.text: All of it is used up in making the water change into steam.
options.rationale: Boiling is the visible end point, and 'used up' is the everyday account of it.

options.text: Most goes to the room and only a little goes into the water.
options.rationale: Students who know some energy escapes overcorrect and assume the escaping share is the larger one.

mcqs.stem: A kettle heats 0.50 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. Using ΔE = m c Δθ, which is given on the Physics equation sheet, how much energy is transferred to the thermal store of the water?

options.rationale: 0.50 × 4200 × 100: the final temperature is used instead of the change.
4200 × 80: the mass is left out because c is thought to cover the whole sample.
ΔE = 0.50 × 4200 × 80 = 168 000 J, using the temperature change of 80 °C.
0.50 × 4200 × 20: the starting temperature is used instead of the change.

mcqs.stem: 0.40 kg of cooking oil is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C. The specific heat capacity of the oil is 2000 J/kg °C. How much energy is transferred to the thermal store of the oil?

options.rationale: 0.40 × 2000 × 70: the final temperature is used in place of Δθ.
2000 × 50: the mass is omitted from the calculation.
0.40 × 2000 × 20: the starting temperature is used in place of Δθ.

mcqs.stem: A constant force of 20 N moves a box of mass 4.0 kg a distance of 3.0 m along the line of action of the force. How much work is done by the force?

options.rationale: W = F s = 20 × 3.0 = 60 J. The mass is not needed.
20 × 4.0 × 3.0: the mass is multiplied in as well, because it was given.
The work done is taken to be the force itself, with the distance playing no part.
20 ÷ 3.0: the equation is divided rather than multiplied.

mcqs.stem: A student holds a heavy box completely still, at arm's length, for 30 s. How much work is done by the student on the box?

options.text: A large amount, because a big force is needed to hold the box up.
options.rationale: Work is assumed to follow from applying a force, with no requirement to move.

options.text: None, because the box does not move in the direction of the force.
options.rationale: W = F s, and s is zero, so the work done on the box is zero however large the force.

options.text: It depends on the time, because holding it for longer is harder.
options.rationale: The genuine effort in the arm is mistaken for work done on the box; t is not in W = F s.

options.text: It equals the weight of the box multiplied by the arm's length.
options.rationale: A distance is present in the situation, so it is used even though the box never travelled it.

mcqs.stem: An electric heater has a power of 2000 W and is switched on for 3.0 minutes. Using P = E/t, how much energy is transferred by the heater?

options.rationale: 2000 × 3: the time is left in minutes rather than converted to seconds.
2000 ÷ 3: the division in P = E/t is kept when rearranging.
E = P t = 2000 × 180 = 360 000 J, with the time converted to seconds.
180 ÷ 2000: the rearrangement is inverted, giving time divided by power.

mcqs.stem: A current flows through the heating element of a kettle. Which statement describes what is happening?

options.text: Electrical energy is stored in the element as current flows.
options.rationale: 'Electrical energy' is treated as a store rather than as a way of transferring energy.

options.text: The current is used up as it passes through the hot element.
options.rationale: Something is clearly consumed at the element, and current is confused with energy.

options.text: The element creates energy from the current flowing inside it.
options.rationale: Heating is treated as a substance the element manufactures out of electricity.

options.text: Work is done, and the thermal store of the element fills.
options.rationale: This is the specification's route: work done when a current flows fills a thermal store.

mcqs.stem: While boiling water, a kettle element transfers 180 000 J. Of this, 168 000 J fills the thermal store of the water and 9 000 J fills the thermal store of the kettle body. On a common scale, how much is shown transferred to the surroundings?

options.rationale: 180 000 − 168 000 − 9 000 = 3 000 J, so the amounts after add up to the amount before.
180 000 − 168 000: the kettle body is left out of the accounting.
12 000 + 9 000: the body's share is added on, so the amounts after exceed the amount before.
A value already given in the question is repeated instead of being subtracted.

mcqs.stem: A bar chart on a common scale shows the energy in each store of a system before and after it changes. What should be true of the bars?

options.text: The bars after add up to less, because energy is used up.
options.rationale: Energy is thought to be consumed, so the totals are not expected to balance.

options.text: The bars after add up to the same total as the bars before.
options.rationale: The energy is redistributed among the stores, so the totals match; that is what the common scale shows.

options.text: Every bar after the change is smaller than it was before.
options.rationale: 'Energy runs down' is applied to every store at once, ignoring the ones that fill.

options.text: The bars are drawn on separate scales so all can be seen.
options.rationale: Chart-drawing habits from other subjects override the instruction to use a common scale.
